overview.title: The encoder-decoder template for seq2seq
overview.main_topic: How sequence-to-sequence models are trained (encoder plus a decoder trained as a language model on the target) and how they generate at inference (start from a [start] seed token and loop until [end]), illustrated by figure 15.1.
overview.central_idea: A seq2seq model is an encoder that summarizes the source plus a decoder that is a conditional language model over the target. In training the decoder sees the true target shifted right by one step. At inference it generates one token at a time from "[start]", feeding its predictions back in until it emits "[end]".
overview.importance: This template underlies both the RNN translator (section 15.2.2) and the Transformer translator (section 15.3.4). The [start]/[end] tokens and the shifted target are the details students most often get wrong when implementing seq2seq.
learning_objectives: Describe the roles of the encoder and decoder in seq2seq training.
Explain what 'the target sequence offset by one step in the future' means, using figure 15.1.
List the three inference steps: encode the source, seed with [start], loop until [end].
Relate seq2seq inference to the Shakespeare generator.
prerequisites: The language-model setup and autoregressive generation (pp.450-452).

summary:
This page gives the **general template** for sequence-to-sequence models, illustrated in **figure 15.1**.

**During training:**

- An **encoder** turns the source sequence (for example, `how, is, the, weather, today`) into an intermediate representation.
- A **decoder** is trained with the **language-modeling setup** from section 15.1. It predicts the next target token by looking at all previous target tokens *and* the encoder's representation of the source. In the figure, the decoder input is `[start], qué, tiempo, hace, hoy` and its training target is `qué, tiempo, hace, hoy, [end]`: the same sequence shifted one step into the future.

**During inference** the target sequence is unknown; it has to be predicted from scratch. It is generated one token at a time, "just as we did with our Shakespeare generator":

1. Get the encoded source sequence from the encoder.
2. The decoder looks at the encoded source and an initial **seed token** such as `"[start]"` and predicts the first real token (in the figure, `qué`).
3. The predicted sequence so far is fed back into the decoder, in a loop, until it generates a **stop token** such as `"[end]"`.

The figure caption summarizes this: the decoder looks at the target sequence so far and predicts the target offset by one step, and during inference each generated token is fed back into the decoder (the curved arrow). The page ends with: "Let's build a sequence-to-sequence translation model."

Compared with the Shakespeare model, the decoder has a second source of information (the encoded source), and generation can stop on its own because the model learned to produce `[end]`.

paragraphs.excerpt: The general template behind sequence-to-sequence models is described in figure 15.1.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Figure 15.1 shows the general seq2seq template; the page first lists what happens during training.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The same two-part structure (encoder and decoder) is used whatever the internals, RNN or Transformer.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets up the vocabulary (encoder, decoder, training phase, inference phase) used through section 15.3.

terminology.meaning: An architecture pattern that stays the same while the components (GRU, Transformer blocks) change.

connections: p.452: seq2seq introduced with translation and question answering as examples.

paragraphs.excerpt: An encoder model turns the source sequence into an intermediate representation.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The encoder converts the source sequence into an intermediate representation.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The encoder reads the whole source, here 'how is the weather today', and produces something the decoder can use: a vector (the final RNN state, p.457) or a sequence of vectors (Transformer encoder outputs, later in the chapter). Because the whole source is available, the encoder may look at it in both directions.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The decoder's output can only be as good as the source information this representation keeps. The limits of a single state vector motivate attention (p.461).

terminology.meaning: The part of a seq2seq model that turns the source sequence into a representation.
The encoded source passed to the decoder.

connections: p.457: the representation can be the RNN's last output or its final state vectors.
p.458: the RNN encoder uses a Bidirectional layer to get a rich source representation.
p.461: one fixed-size state vector limits sentence size and complexity.

paragraphs.excerpt: A decoder is trained using the language modeling setup we saw previously.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The decoder is trained with the language-modeling setup. It recursively predicts the next target token by looking at all previous target tokens and the encoder's representation of the source.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The decoder is a conditional language model: it learns $p(y_t \mid y_{<t}, \text{source})$. Its training input is the true target shifted right with a [start] token at the front, and its labels are the target shifted left with [end] at the end. All positions are trained in parallel on true previous tokens; no predictions are fed back during training.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Because it is a language model over the target, all the earlier lessons apply. In particular the decoder must be causal: p.458 notes that a Bidirectional decoder would make the loss trivially easy, just as on p.452.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The word *and* is italicized on the page: the decoder's prediction combines two sources of information, the target prefix and the encoded source.

terminology.meaning: The part that generates the target sequence token by token, conditioned on the encoded source.
The output sequence to be produced, for example the Spanish translation.

connections: p.452: the language-modeling setup and why it must be causal.
p.458: the decoder GRU takes the encoded source as its initial state; a Bidirectional decoder would break training.

paragraphs.excerpt: During inference, we don’t have access to the target sequence—we’re trying to
paragraphs.what_it_says: At inference the target sequence is not available; it has to be predicted from scratch, one token at a time, as with the Shakespeare generator.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The same train/inference asymmetry as on p.452 applies. Training conditions on the true target prefix; inference conditions on the model's own generated prefix.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains why a seq2seq translator, like the Shakespeare model, needs a separate generation loop rather than a single `predict` call.

terminology.meaning: Using the trained model to produce outputs for new inputs.

connections: p.451: the Shakespeare greedy loop that this procedure mirrors.

paragraphs.excerpt: The decoder starts by looking at the encoded source sequence as well
paragraphs.what_it_says: The decoder starts from the encoded source and an initial seed token such as "[start]", and uses them to predict the first real token.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The [start] token plays the role of the prompt in the Shakespeare example. Every target sequence in training began with [start], so the decoder has learned what usually follows it given a source. This also covers the first bullet: the source is encoded once before the loop.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Without a seed token the decoder would have no input at step 1. The [start] marker is added to each target during data preparation (section 15.2.1).

terminology.meaning: A special token ("[start]") given to the decoder as its first input so it can predict the first real token.

connections: p.451: in the Shakespeare model the prompt primed generation instead.
p.454: section 15.2.1 prepares the English-to-Spanish data.

paragraphs.excerpt: The predicted sequence so far is fed back into the decoder, in
paragraphs.what_it_says: The predicted sequence so far is fed back into the decoder in a loop until it produces a stop token such as "[end]".
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the autoregressive loop, with a learned stopping rule. Because every training target ended with [end], the model learns to emit it when the translation is complete. The Shakespeare loop instead ran for a fixed 250 characters.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: A learned stop token lets output length vary with input. In practice a maximum length is still added as a safeguard in case [end] never appears.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note that the bullet says the predicted sequence so far is fed back, the whole prefix. A model without carried state reprocesses that prefix at every step; p.461 notes this is inefficient and that the RNN state could be cached instead.

terminology.meaning: A special token ("[end]") marking the end of the generated sequence.

connections: p.461: the simple inference setup reprocesses the whole source and generated target each step.
p.451: fixed-length generation loop for comparison.

paragraphs.excerpt: Figure 15.1 Sequence-to-sequence learning: the source sequence is processed by the encoder
paragraphs.what_it_says: Figure caption: the encoder processes the source and passes it to the decoder. The decoder looks at the target so far and predicts the target offset by one step into the future. At inference one target token is generated at a time and fed back into the decoder.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Training panel: encoder input 'how, is, the, weather, today'; decoder input '[start], qué, tiempo, hace, hoy'; decoder output 'qué, tiempo, hace, hoy, [end]'. Each output position is the next token of the input. Inference panel: decoder input '[start]' gives 'qué', and a curved arrow shows 'qué' being fed back.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The shift by one position is the key to building seq2seq training data and is exactly the trick used for Shakespeare (labels = inputs offset by one, p.447).

terminology.meaning: The label at position t is the input at position t+1.

connections: p.447: the same offset trick for the character-level language model.

concepts.name: Encoder-decoder architecture
concepts.definition: A seq2seq model made of an encoder that represents the source sequence and a decoder that generates the target sequence conditioned on that representation.
concepts.intuition: A translator first reads and understands the sentence (encoder), then writes the translation word by word (decoder).
concepts.technical: Encoder: $z = \mathrm{Enc}(x_1..x_n)$. Decoder: $p(y_t\mid y_{<t}, z)$, trained with the shifted target and run autoregressively at inference.
concepts.significance: It is the standard design for translation and the original Transformer architecture.
concepts.example: Figure 15.1: 'how is the weather today' becomes 'qué tiempo hace hoy'.
concepts.misconception: That the decoder can see the whole target during training. It sees the full prefix at each position but never tokens at or after the one it predicts.

concepts.name: Sequence-to-sequence learning
concepts.definition: Learning to map a source sequence to a target sequence; the decoder learns the next target token given past target tokens and the source.
concepts.significance: It covers translation, question answering and summarization.
concepts.misconception: That source and target must have equal length; here 5 English tokens map to 4 Spanish tokens plus [end].

concepts.name: [start] and [end] tokens
concepts.definition: Special tokens added to target sequences: [start] seeds generation and [end] signals that generation should stop.
concepts.technical: Decoder input = [start] + target; decoder label = target + [end]. At inference, begin with [start] and stop when [end] is the argmax (or at a maximum length).
concepts.significance: They let a model generate variable-length outputs and know when to stop.
concepts.example: '[start] qué tiempo hace hoy' as input, 'qué tiempo hace hoy [end]' as labels.
concepts.misconception: That [end] removes the need for a maximum length. A model may never emit it, so a cap is still sensible.

concepts.name: Training on the shifted true target
concepts.definition: Feeding the decoder the true previous target tokens during training rather than its own predictions.
concepts.intuition: Training wheels: the correct prefix is always provided.
concepts.technical: All target positions are computed in parallel from the true prefix. Beyond the book: this is called teacher forcing.
concepts.significance: It makes training efficient and stable, at the cost of a train/inference mismatch.
concepts.example: Figure 15.1's training panel feeds '[start], qué, tiempo, hace, hoy' regardless of what the decoder would have predicted.
concepts.misconception: That the model's own predictions are used during training. They are not (p.452).

math.title: Seq2seq decoder objective
math.latex: p(y_1,\dots,y_m \mid x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{t=1}^{m} p\big(y_t \mid y_0,\dots,y_{t-1},\ \operatorname{Enc}(x_1,\dots,x_n)\big),\quad y_0=\texttt{[start]},\ y_m=\texttt{[end]}
math.source_text: Described in words: the decoder predicts the next token in the target sequence by looking at all previous target tokens and the encoder's representation of the source sequence.

variables.meaning: source tokens (how, is, the, weather, today)
the encoder, producing the intermediate representation

math.operations: Chain-rule factorization of the target conditioned on the source.
math.purpose: It states what the decoder learns and what inference generates step by step.
math.interpretation: A language model over the target that also always sees the encoded source.
math.intuition: Each Spanish word is chosen from what has been written so far plus the meaning of the English sentence.
math.numerical_example: For figure 15.1, m = 5 factors: p(qué|[start],x)·p(tiempo|[start] qué,x)·p(hace|…)·p(hoy|…)·p([end]|…).

deeper.title: Building the training pair from figure 15.1
deeper.body:
1. Source: `how is the weather today` goes to the encoder.
2. Target sentence: `qué tiempo hace hoy`.
3. Decoder input: prepend [start], giving `[start] qué tiempo hace hoy`.
4. Decoder labels: append [end], giving `qué tiempo hace hoy [end]`.
5. Position by position: [start] predicts qué, qué predicts tiempo, tiempo predicts hace, hace predicts hoy, hoy predicts [end].

This is the same one-step offset used for Shakespeare (p.447), with an encoder added.

deeper.title: Shakespeare generator versus seq2seq decoder
deeper.body:
| | Shakespeare LM (p.451) | Seq2seq decoder (p.453) |
|---|---|---|
| Conditioning | prompt text | encoded source + [start] |
| Starting input | prompt characters | [start] |
| Stopping | fixed 250 steps | [end] token |
| Training input | true previous characters | true previous target tokens |

deeper.title: Analogy: a court interpreter
deeper.body: The interpreter first listens to the whole sentence (encoder). Then they start speaking (seed) and say one word at a time while remembering both the original sentence and what they have already said (decoder looking at the encoded source and its own prefix). They stop when the thought is complete ([end]).

misconceptions.claim: At inference the decoder receives the reference translation, as it does in training.
misconceptions.correction: At inference the target is unknown; the decoder gets [start] and then its own predictions.

misconceptions.claim: The decoder output at position t is the token at position t of its input.
misconceptions.correction: It is the next token: the output is offset one step into the future.

misconceptions.claim: The encoder must also be causal like the decoder.
misconceptions.correction: The source is fully known, so the encoder may read it in both directions (p.458 uses a Bidirectional encoder). Only the decoder must be causal.

related_math.note: Seq2seq language model: next token given past target tokens and a fixed source sequence.

takeaways: Seq2seq = encoder (source to representation) + decoder (a conditional language model over the target).
In training, the decoder input is [start] + target and its labels are target + [end]: offset by one step.
The decoder conditions on all previous target tokens and the encoded source.
Inference: encode the source, seed the decoder with [start], feed predictions back until [end].
This is the Shakespeare generation loop with an extra conditioning input and a learned stop token.

questions.question: In figure 15.1's training phase, what is the decoder's target output?
questions.explanation: The decoder predicts the target offset by one step. The first option is the decoder's input, the third is the encoder's input, and the fourth is neither.

questions.question: What are the roles of "[start]" and "[end]" in seq2seq inference?
questions.answer: [start] is the seed token given to the decoder to predict the first real token; [end] is the stop token whose generation ends the loop.
questions.explanation: Both are described in the inference bullets on the page.

questions.question: In what sense is the seq2seq decoder 'trained using the language modeling setup we saw previously'? What is different?
questions.answer: Like the Shakespeare model, it predicts the next token from all previous (true) tokens, with labels shifted by one. The difference is that it also conditions on the encoder's representation of a separate source sequence.
questions.explanation: The italicized *and* on the page stresses the two sources of information.

questions.question: Which component may legitimately read its input in both directions?
questions.explanation: The source is fully known, so the encoder can be bidirectional (p.458). The decoder is a language model, and future target tokens would leak the label (p.452, p.458).

questions.question: Why can the seq2seq generation loop stop by itself while the Shakespeare loop ran for a fixed 250 steps?
questions.answer: Every training target ends with [end], so the decoder learns to predict it when the output is complete. The Shakespeare model was trained on continuous chunks with no end marker.
questions.explanation: The stop token is part of the training labels.

questions.question: For the figure's example, how many next-token predictions does the decoder make per training example, and how many inference loop iterations are needed if every prediction is correct?
questions.answer: 5 predictions in training (qué, tiempo, hace, hoy, [end]); 5 inference iterations, the last producing [end].
questions.explanation: The decoder input has 5 tokens and so does the shifted label sequence.

questions.question: Without looking at the figure, can you write the decoder input and labels for translating 'I am hungry' to 'tengo hambre'?
questions.answer: Decoder input: [start] tengo hambre. Labels: tengo hambre [end]. Encoder input: I am hungry.
questions.explanation: Apply the one-step offset with the special tokens.
